title: Detecting Action-Items in E-mail
research_question: Does using fine-grained sentence-level action-item annotation improve automatic detection of action-item e-mails compared with document-level annotation, and which text representations work best for the task?
methodology: The authors collected 744 non-duplicate e-mails from university volunteers, manually removed quoted material, and had two annotators identify action-item segments; after reconciliation, 328 messages contained action-items, with kappa of 0.85 at document level and 0.82 at sentence level. They compared document-level and sentence-level classifiers using unigram and n-gram representations with k-NN, multinomial naive Bayes, and SVM models; automatically segmented sentences were labeled positive when they contained at least 30% of a marked action-item segment. Sentence predictions were aggregated to document predictions by marking a document positive if any sentence was positive. Evaluation used 10-fold document-level cross-validation, nested feature selection, F1 and accuracy, and two-tailed t-tests at p=0.05.

key_findings.finding: Sentence-level classifiers generally produced better document-level action-item detection than classifiers trained directly on whole e-mails; the advantage was significant for the reported comparisons except SVM F1.
N-gram features improved document-level performance for k-NN and SVM and yielded the strongest document-level representations, while multinomial naive Bayes was hurt by n-gram double-counting.
The best reported document-detection F1 was 0.7790 for the sentence-level n-gram k-NN system, while the best reported document accuracy was 0.8173 for the sentence-level n-gram SVM system.
At sentence granularity, unigrams approached n-gram performance because the short sentence window already captured much of the local lexical-pattern information supplied explicitly by n-grams.

Direct sentence detection achieved accuracy around 0.94-0.96 but substantially lower F1 around 0.62-0.67, indicating that the positive action-item class remained considerably harder than overall accuracy alone suggests.
The formulation explicitly treats action-item detection as recovering whether the sender intends to elicit an action or response and localizing the text expressing that request.

limitations: The corpus contains only 744 e-mails collected from volunteers at one university, so generalization to diverse organizations, industries, languages, and modern workplace chat is not established.
Only the body of each e-mail was used; sender, recipient, timestamps, and other header information were excluded.
Quoted material was removed manually, so the experiments do not test realistic handling of complete conversational threads or inline replies.
The task detects whether an e-mail or sentence contains an action-item but does not decompose it into owner, action/object, deadline, conditions, status, or other structured fields.
The study does not separately model requests, commitments, decisions, promises, or other speech-act subclasses that may underlie an action-item.

The main sentence-versus-document comparison evaluates document detection after a simple any-positive-sentence aggregation rule, rather than evaluating richer cross-sentence or thread-level reasoning.
Automatic sentence segmentation and the rule that a sentence is positive when it contains at least 30% of an annotated action-item segment introduce task-specific preprocessing assumptions.
The paper notes that associated user studies are omitted, so improved classification metrics are not directly tied to measured productivity or task-completion benefits.
raw_claims: Action-item detection seeks both to identify e-mails requiring action or response and to highlight the text expressing the request.
The authors treat sender intent to elicit a receiver response or action as central to the task.
They formulate three system problems: document detection, document ranking, and sentence detection.
The experimental corpus contains 744 e-mail messages after duplicate removal.
Two annotators marked action-item segments, with reported kappa of 0.85 for document judgments and 0.82 for sentence judgments.
After annotation reconciliation, 328 e-mails were considered to contain action-items.
The experiments compare k-NN, multinomial naive Bayes, and SVM classifiers with unigram and n-gram representations.
N-grams improve document-level results for most classifiers but degrade multinomial naive Bayes in these experiments.
Sentence-level classifiers outperform their document-level counterparts in most reported document-detection comparisons.
At sentence level, a unigram representation performs almost as well as n-grams because the local context window is already small.
The best reported document-level F1 is 0.7790 and the best reported document-level accuracy is 0.8173.
